q: A colourless liquid is added to anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride paper and the paper changes colour. Which change shows that the liquid contains water?
explain: Anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride is blue and turns pink when water is added.

q: What happens to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate when water is added to it?
options: It turns from blue to white.
It turns from blue to pink.
It turns from white to blue.
It turns from pink to blue.
explain: Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is white; hydrated copper(II) sulfate is blue.

q: Which row correctly gives the colour change when water is detected?
explain: Cobalt(II) chloride goes blue to pink; copper(II) sulfate goes white to blue.

q: What is the boiling point of pure water at normal atmospheric pressure?
explain: Pure water boils at 100 °C at normal pressure.

q: A student wants to show that a sample of water is pure. Which result would be the best evidence?
options: It turns anhydrous copper(II) sulfate blue.
It is colourless and has no smell.
It melts at exactly 0 °C and boils at exactly 100 °C.
It boils at 100 °C but melts over a range of temperatures.
explain: Pure substances have sharp, fixed melting and boiling points. The copper(II) sulfate test only shows that water is present.

q: A colourless liquid turns anhydrous copper(II) sulfate blue. Which conclusion is correct?
options: The liquid contains water but may not be pure water.
The liquid contains no dissolved substances.
explain: The test only detects water. Salt solution or other mixtures containing water give the same result.

q: A sample of water freezes at −2 °C and boils at 102 °C. What does this show?
options: The water contains dissolved oxygen only.
explain: Impurities lower the melting point and raise the boiling point, so the sample is not pure water.

q: Why is distilled water used in practical chemistry rather than tap water?
options: It is always at a lower temperature.
It is a better solvent for ionic compounds.
explain: Tap water contains dissolved substances that could react with the chemicals used or change results.

q: Which substance in natural water is beneficial to aquatic life?
explain: Fish and other aquatic animals need dissolved oxygen to respire.

q: Which statement about metal compounds in natural water is correct?
options: Some provide essential minerals but some are toxic.
All of them are harmful to living things.
All of them are needed for life.
None of them is found in natural water.
explain: Some metal compounds supply minerals needed by living things, while others, such as lead compounds, are toxic.

q: Which statement about sewage in water is correct?
options: It increases the dissolved oxygen needed by fish.
It contains harmful microbes that cause disease.
It is removed from water by adding anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.
It is the main source of phosphates from fertilisers.
explain: Sewage contains microbes that can cause diseases such as cholera.

q: What is a harmful effect of plastics in water?
options: They remove nitrates from the water.
They increase the dissolved oxygen concentration.
They kill all microbes in the water.
explain: Animals can swallow plastics or become trapped in them, which damages aquatic life.

q: Nitrates and phosphates from fertilisers run into a river. What is the main harmful effect on the river?
options: The river becomes more acidic and all metals dissolve.
The concentration of dissolved oxygen increases.
The water becomes deoxygenated and aquatic life is damaged.
explain: Excess nitrates and phosphates lead to deoxygenation of the water, which damages aquatic life.

q: Which substances in natural water come from fertilisers?
explain: Fertilisers supply nitrogen as nitrates and phosphorus as phosphates, which wash into water.

q: Which source gives phosphates in natural water?
explain: Phosphates enter water from fertilisers and from detergents.

q: What is the purpose of the sedimentation and filtration stages in treating the domestic water supply?
explain: Sedimentation lets large solids settle and filtration removes smaller solids.

q: Why is carbon used in the treatment of domestic water?
options: to add chlorine to the water
explain: Carbon adsorbs the substances that cause unpleasant tastes and smells.

q: Why is chlorine added to the domestic water supply?
explain: Chlorination kills microbes that could cause disease.

q: Which row correctly matches each water treatment stage with its purpose?
explain: Filtration removes solids; carbon removes tastes and smells; chlorine kills microbes.

q: Which list gives the stages of domestic water treatment in the correct order?
explain: Solids are removed first, then carbon removes tastes and odours, and chlorine is added to kill microbes.

q: A student tests a liquid for water. Which test is suitable?
options: Add damp litmus paper and see if it turns blue.
Add silver nitrate solution and look for a white solid.
Heat the liquid and see if it burns with a pop.
Add anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride and see if it turns pink.
explain: Anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride is blue and turns pink in the presence of water.

q: What does a sharp melting point of a solid show?
explain: Pure substances melt at one fixed temperature; impure substances melt over a range of temperatures.

q: Which statement about distillation of natural water is correct?
options: It removes dissolved solids because they stay behind when the water evaporates.
It adds dissolved oxygen to the water.
It leaves the dissolved solids in the distillate.
It increases the number of microbes in the water.
explain: Water evaporates and condenses; dissolved solids are left behind, giving distilled water.

q: Why must the domestic water supply be treated before drinking?
options: to remove all the dissolved oxygen
to make it contain only hydrogen and oxygen
to remove solids and kill harmful microbes
explain: Raw water contains solids and microbes that can cause disease.

q: Which description of anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride is correct?
options: It is blue and used to test for water.
It is pink and used to test for water.
It is white and used to test for water.
It is blue and used to test for oxygen.
explain: Anhydrous cobalt(II) chloride is blue; it turns pink when water is present.

q: A student boils a liquid and the thermometer reading rises steadily from 98 °C to 104 °C. What is the best conclusion?
options: The liquid is a pure element.
The liquid contains only dissolved oxygen.
The liquid is a mixture, not a pure substance.
explain: A pure liquid boils at one fixed temperature, so a steady rise through a range means a mixture.

q: A dissolved impurity is added to pure water. How do the melting and boiling points change?
options: The melting point is raised and the boiling point is lowered.
The melting point is lowered and the boiling point is raised.
explain: Impurities lower the melting point and raise the boiling point compared with the pure substance.

q: Which row correctly shows an effect of each substance in natural water?
options: sewage | provides oxygen for aquatic life
explain: Fish use dissolved oxygen; sewage and plastics are pollutants and phosphates cause deoxygenation.

q: Which statement about the effect of nitrates and phosphates on a lake is correct?
options: They lead to deoxygenation of the water, which damages aquatic life.
They increase the oxygen concentration so fish grow faster.
They kill microbes in the lake.
They convert sewage into harmless solids.
explain: Extra nutrients lead to deoxygenation of the water, damaging aquatic life.

q: Why is chlorination carried out after the filtration stage rather than before it?
options: Chlorine would turn into carbon if added earlier.
Filtration produces the microbes that must be killed.
Solids are removed first so the chlorine can kill microbes more effectively.
explain: Removing solids first leaves cleaner water so that chlorine can reach and kill microbes more effectively.
